# Financial Effects of an Out-of-Pocket Cap in Traditional Medicare

**Authors:** Andrew M. Ryan; Meehir N. Dixit; Mathew M. Maughan; David J. Meyers; Fangli Geng

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Health Services, Policy, and Practice, Brown University School of Public Health, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island | 2University of Chicago Pritzker School of Medicine, Chicago, Illinois

## Abstract

This economic evaluation assesses the financial outcomes of an out-of-pocket spending cap in traditional Medicare for Parts A and B.

## Abstract

What are the projected financial impacts of introducing an out-of-pocket (OOP) spending cap in traditional Medicare (TM) for Parts A and B?

In this economic evaluation using principles of microsimulation analysis of projected Medicare enrollment and spending from 2026 to 2034, an OOP cap of $3000 annually was estimated to reduce beneficiary spending by $1568 per year, a cap of $5000 annually by $1138 per year, and a cap of $10 000 annually by $707 per year, while increasing annual Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services expenditures by $96 billion, $70 billion, and $39 billion.

These findings suggest that implementing an OOP cap in TM would offer substantial financial protection for beneficiaries but impose substantial federal costs; a $10 000 cap may best balance affordability with fiscal sustainability.

## Abstract

Traditional Medicare (TM) exposes beneficiaries to substantial financial risk because, unlike Medicare Advantage (MA), there is no out-of-pocket (OOP) maximum for medical spending. Policymakers have proposed introducing an OOP cap, but its fiscal and behavioral effects are uncertain.

To estimate the financial impacts of introducing OOP spending caps of $3000, $5000, or $10 000 annually in TM on beneficiary costs, enrollment patterns, and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services expenditures between 2026 and 2034.

This economic evaluation using principles of microsimulation analysis projected enrollment, spending, and health care use outcomes under baseline (no OOP cap) and 3 alternative cap scenarios using publicly available national Medicare and insurance data from 2020 to 2024 with projections through 2034. The model incorporated elasticity-based behavioral responses, including beneficiary switching between TM and MA, changes in service use, and increases to MA benchmarks and spending. Sensitivity analyses varied model assumptions probabilistically.

Introduction of annual OOP caps for Parts A and B in TM at $3000, $5000, or $10 000.

Projected changes in beneficiary enrollment by coverage type, mean annual beneficiary OOP and premium spending, and annual Medicare expenditures.

Between 2026 and 2034, a $3000 OOP cap was projected to reduce mean annual beneficiary expenditures by $1568, compared with $1138 under a $5000 cap and $707 under a $10 000 cap. Corresponding increases in annual Medicare spending were estimated at $96 billion (90% simulation uncertainty interval [SUI], $80-$114 billion), $70 billion (90% SUI, $55-$85 billion), and $39 billion (90% SUI, $29-$50 billion), respectively. OOP caps, especially at lower thresholds, would substantially shift beneficiaries from MA to TM.

Results of this study suggest that implementing an OOP spending cap in TM would provide meaningful financial protection for beneficiaries but impose substantial fiscal costs on Medicare.

## Introduction

Over half of Medicare beneficiaries are now enrolled in Medicare Advantage (MA).1 Beneficiaries are increasingly choosing MA plans because they offer supplemental benefits (including prescription drugs, vision, dental, and hearing) and cost sharing protections, all at premiums that are substantially lower than in traditional Medicare (TM).2 Beneficiaries’ relative ease of one stop shopping for MA—choosing a single plan that covers all their benefits as opposed to piecing together Medigap and stand-alone prescription drug plans in TM – has also likely contributed to the shift toward MA. In parallel, employer groups have moved away from offering retiree coverage that supplements TM and shifted toward employer-sponsored MA plans.3,4

Despite the growing popularity of MA, it has important limitations that affect access to care and the quality of coverage. For beneficiaries, these include network restrictions, frequent denials and prior authorization requirements, and supplemental benefits that often fall short of marketing claims.5,6 From a fiscal perspective, MA also places a growing burden on the federal budget: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) pays MA plans 20% more to care for a similar beneficiary in TM due to overpayments from excessive risk coding, favorable selection, generous quality bonus payments, and other payment distortions.2,7,8,9,10

In this context, beneficiary advocates, policymakers, and policy analysts have increasingly discussed ways to even the playing field between TM and MA. One policy under consideration is to offer an out-of-pocket (OOP) spending cap in TM for Parts A and B.11,12 OOP spending caps are nearly universal health insurance benefit features in both public and private coverage, serving as a critical financial protection against catastrophic medical costs.13 However, OOP caps have been noticeably absent from the TM program. While the Inflation Reduction Act recently introduced an OOP cap for prescription drug spending under Part D, there is no such protection in Parts A and B. The absence of an OOP cap in TM exposes beneficiaries, especially those without supplemental coverage, to substantial financial risk and represents a critical policy gap in Medicare’s structure. Conversely, MA plans are required to offer such an OOP cap on medical spending, creating a substantial advantage that draws beneficiaries away from TM. An OOP cap in TM can be seen as an effort to improve benefit comparability and preserve beneficiary choice, while highlighting concerns about the fiscal impacts of continued beneficiary migration to MA.

Although an OOP cap for Parts A and B has conceptual appeal, its financial impacts for beneficiaries and CMS are unknown. Under an OOP spending cap, Medicare would assume financial responsibility for all beneficiary spending related to Part A and B above the cap. This would lead to transfer of financial risk from beneficiaries to CMS, with potentially substantial implications for Medicare spending. At the same time, an OOP spending cap in TM could lead to a complex set of behavioral interactions among beneficiaries and health plans. This includes beneficiary switching between MA and TM and changes in cost sharing, health care use, and spending. We used a microsimulation model to estimate the impacts of an OOP cap for Parts A and B in TM in financial outcomes. We assess both the distributional impacts for beneficiaries and the aggregate fiscal implications for CMS.

## Methods

This study used publicly available data and did not include any direct interaction with or intervention involving human participants. As a result, the research qualified for exemption from institutional review board (IRB) review. Because this study used the principles of microsimulation, no established reporting guideline was directly applicable.

We developed a microsimulation model to project the financial impacts of 3 potential annual OOP Part A and Part B spending caps ($3000, $5000, $10 000) for TM beneficiaries between 2026 and 2034. Our model simulated enrollment segments within the Medicare population over time and updated enrollment, spending, and use outcomes annually in response to policy-induced changes in premiums and cost sharing. Behavioral responses were incorporated through elasticity-based switching between coverage types and price responsiveness in health care use. The model therefore tracked how the initiation of OOP caps propagates through the simulated population and generated projected outcomes over time, which is consistent with standard microsimulation approaches used in health policy analysis.14

We modeled the impacts of OOP caps at varying levels of generosity relative to the current OOP cap in MA (around $5000 for in-network care and $9000 total).15 Estimates of spending and enrollment with no OOP cap (the baseline scenario) were based on projections between 2026 and 2034 (expressed in 2024 dollars) from the 2025 Medicare Trustees Report.16

We modeled enrollment and spending separately across key insurance segments within TM (no supplemental insurance, employer-sponsored supplemental insurance, Medigap-individually purchased supplemental insurance, and TM-dual eligibility with Medicaid) and MA (individual MA, employer-sponsored MA, and MA enrollees with dual eligibility) using data on the share of beneficiaries in each segment.4 Relative spending differences, cost sharing, and spending above various OOP caps across segments were based on the 2021 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey and recent literature.17 Medigap premiums and loss ratios were calculated using data from 2020 to 2024 from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, accessed through the Mark Farrah portal.18 These data were combined with Trustee estimates of Medicare spending growth to estimate future Medigap premiums.

### Microsimulation Model Design

Our microsimulation model was constructed at the segment-year level (eg, Medigap, no supplemental insurance, individually purchased MA, in 2026). The model was implemented in several steps. First, the baseline scenario was established based on CMS actuary reports and Congressional Budget Office models. Second, an OOP cap in TM was assigned at 1 of 3 levels: $3000, $5000, and $10 000. The cap decreased Medigap premiums because Medigap plans would no longer be responsible for OOP spending above the cap (which would be covered by Medicare). Based on new Medigap premiums and beneficiaries’ cross price elasticity of demand, beneficiaries (and their employers) decided whether to switch from no supplemental coverage to TM plus Medigap; switch from MA to TM plus Medigap; or remain in their current coverage. No beneficiaries switched to MA nor did they drop Medigap and remain in TM. Consistent with evidence related to plan choice in other settings, the switching phased in over time as beneficiaries became aware of the OOP caps.19,20,21 Differences in effective cost sharing resulting both from the OOP caps and from plan switching were translated into use changes through assumptions about the price elasticity of demand for health care. Changes to MA spending, resulting from higher benchmarks from increases in TM spending, were also incorporated (eMethods in Supplement 1). Outputs from the simulation were then captured, including paid Medigap premiums, OOP spending, Part B premiums paid by beneficiaries, Medicare expenditures, and Part B premiums received by CMS (Box).

To characterize uncertainty in model estimates related to Medicare expenditures and beneficiary savings, we conducted a probabilistic sensitivity analysis in which key behavioral parameters were varied simultaneously across plausible ranges (eTable 1 in Supplement 1). We repeated the simulation 10 000 times and calculated 90% simulation uncertainty intervals using the 5th and 95th percentiles of the simulated outcome distribution. We then used regression analysis to assess the association of specific parameters and Medicare expenditures. This analysis varied the price elasticity of demand for medical care, the own price elasticity of demand for Medigap, the cross-price elasticity of demand for MA with respect to Medigap premiums, the cost differential between TM and MA, and the extent to which higher TM spending would increase MA spending. More detailed information on the simulation and assumptions is described in the eMethods, eTable 1, eTable 2, eFigure 1, and eFigure 2 in Supplement 1. Simulation model and statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 18 (StataCorp LLC).

### Enrollment Effects of OOP Caps

Figure 1 shows the projected impacts for 3 alternative OOPs for TM and MA enrollment between 2026 and 2034. It shows that the caps would substantially affect beneficiary enrollment decisions, shifting beneficiaries from MA to TM. Under the $3000 cap, TM enrollment was projected to be greater than MA enrollment until 2034 when enrollment would be equal. Under the $5000 cap, MA and TM enrollment growth were projected to be similar until 2030, after which MA enrollment growth would exceed that of TM. Under the $10 000 cap, MA enrollment was projected to be greater than TM enrollment through 2034 (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1). Variation in TM and MA enrollment across the cap levels was driven by beneficiaries switching from having no supplemental coverage or MA to Medigap because of lower Medigap premiums (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1).

### Impacts of OOP Caps in Beneficiary Expenditures

Figure 2 shows the estimated impacts of OOP caps for beneficiary expenditures. The $3000, $5000, and $10 000 OOP caps would reduce annual beneficiary expenditures by a mean of $1568, $1138, and $707, respectively, between 2026 and 2034. OOP spending reductions accounted for approximately 68% of gross beneficiary savings with Medigap premium reductions accounting for the remaining 32%. Beneficiary expenditure reductions in TM would increase substantially over time in line with Medicare spending increases. We estimated that the actuarial values of TM with the $3000, $5000, and $10 000 OOPs are 87.9%, 86.8%, and 85.6%, respectively, compared with an actuarial value of 84% of the standard TM benefit.22 Across beneficiaries in TM and MA, the $3000, $5000, and $10 000 OOP caps would increase Part B premiums by $164, $113, and $61, respectively, per member per year.

### Implications of OOP Caps for Federal Spending

The $3000, $5000, and $10 000 OOP caps were projected to increase CMS annual expenditures by $96 billion (90% simulation uncertainty interval [SUI], $80 to $114 billion), $70 billion (90% SUI, $55 to $85 billion), and $39 billion (90% SUI: $29 to $50 billion) between 2026 and 2034 (Figure 3). Approximately 72% of the increase in CMS expenditures from an OOP cap occurred in TM, while the remaining 28% occurred in MA (eFigure 4 in Supplement 1). Also, of the additional CMS expenditures for the $3000, $5000, and $10 000 OOP caps, 9.9%, 8.0%, and 3.6% occurred below the caps because of beneficiaries switching into supplemental coverage with lower cost sharing.

### Sensitivity Analysis

Results were most sensitive to assumptions regarding the own-price elasticity of demand for medical care and the extent to which TM spending increases were passed through to MA (eTable 3 in Supplement 1). Varying medical care elasticity across its plausible range changed projected annual CMS expenditures by $44 billion under a $3000 cap, $38 billion under a $5000 cap, and $27 billion under a $10 000 cap. Assumptions regarding the share of TM spending increases that would be passed through to higher MA spending had a large effect on estimates, changing projected annual CMS expenditures by $27 billion under a $3000 cap, $20 billion under a $5000 cap, and $12 billion under a $10 000 cap. In addition, varying assumptions about the cross-price elasticity of MA enrollment with respect to Medigap premiums and the TM to MA ratio changed projected annual CMS expenditures by $9 billion under a $3000 cap, $14 billion under a $5000 cap, and $17 billion under a $10 000 cap. In contrast, varying the own-price elasticity of Medigap demand changed projected CMS expenditures by $1 billion or less annually across all cap levels.

## Discussion

Our microsimulation model on the projected impacts of OOP spending caps in TM between 2016-2034 yielded 3 key findings. First, OOP caps, particularly the more generous $3000 and $5000 caps, were projected to substantially shift beneficiaries from MA to TM. Second, beneficiary savings from TM OOP caps were projected to be considerable, ranging from a mean annual savings of $1568 for the $3000 OOP cap (3.6% of median per capita income among Medicare beneficiaries) to $707 for the $10 000 OOP cap (1.6% of median per capita income).23 Savings would accrue to all TM beneficiaries (and their employers) who purchase supplemental coverage and also to those whose OOP spending exceeded the cap. For instance, approximately 11% of TM beneficiaries would be expected to hit a $5000 OOP cap in a given year. Third, OOP caps were projected to be expensive, leading to mean annual increases in CMS expenditures under the base scenario of $96 billion for the $3000 OOP cap and $39 billion for the $10 000 OOP cap. The projected implications of OOP spending caps on CMS expenditures were most sensitive to assumptions about elasticity of demand for medical care.

Our research updates and extends other estimates of the impact of OOP caps in Medicare. An Urban Institute report analyzed the impact of introducing a $5000 cap on Parts A, B, and D spending,12 finding that it would increase CMS expenditures by $39 billion in 2023. Although the Urban Institute analysis differs from ours because it includes a Part D spending cap and does not model enrollment shifts or increases in MA spending, the direction and magnitude of the findings are consistent. In both the Urban Institute and our analysis, OOP caps increase federal spending while reducing beneficiary liability and exerting downward pressure on Medigap premiums. The larger Medicare expenditures observed in our analysis likely reflect the later projection period and continued growth in Medicare spending.

Our findings are also consistent with Congressional Budget Office estimates from other Medicare policy settings, including the Medicare Part D redesign enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act, which projected higher federal spending as beneficiary financial liability was reduced through the introduction of an annual OOP cap.24 While a separate analysis by the Congressional Budget Office examined the impact of an OOP cap for Part A and B as part of broader Medicare reforms, their approach did not identify the independent effect of an OOP cap.25 To put the magnitude to our estimates of the impacts of an OOP cap in CMS expenditures, they are relatively close to the costs of adding dental, vision, and hearing care to TM, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would average $35.8 billion per year from 2020 to 2029.26

### Policy Implications

Our findings suggest that OOP caps in TM would have substantial impacts for enrollment patterns, CMS expenditures, and beneficiary savings. Nonetheless, the caps are quite costly and would face an uphill battle legislatively, as seen through other recently proposed benefit enhancements in Medicare.26 Under statutory pay-as-you-go rules, increases in mandatory Medicare spending are generally required to be fully offset over both 5- and 10-year budget windows. As a result, OOP caps would likely require substantial offsets or accompanying benefit or financing reforms to satisfy budget neutrality. Spending offsets to support an OOP payment cap could come through site neutral payment reform, targeted reductions in overpayments to MA plans, estimated to be over $84 billion a year, or other strategies.27,28

In addition to supporting Medicare beneficiaries, OOP caps would also substantially benefit health care clinicians and hospitals. A large share of high OOP costs is never paid to clinicians and hospitals and turn into uncollected liability.29 While CMS pays for a portion of this bad debt, OOP caps would reduce clinicians and hospitals’ administrative burden when seeking payment from beneficiaries and reduce an important part of payment uncertainty.

### Limitations

Our study has several limitations. First, our model considered only the financial benefits to beneficiaries and did not incorporate important benefits for beneficiaries outside of financial savings. Evidence of beneficiary switching implies utility gains to beneficiaries even when beneficiary spending may increase (eg, if a beneficiary switches from no supplemental insurance to Medigap and then pays Medigap premiums). Beneficiary health may also improve through increased use of care. A more complete welfare analysis would incorporate utility gains from an OOP cap, including those resulting from greater financial security, improved mental health,30 and avoiding the hassle and restrained choice from network restrictions and prior authorization in MA.31

Second, our model did not incorporate a comprehensive demand function for health insurance, which includes many relevant features related to supplemental benefits, network preferences, cost sharing, and price along with beneficiaries’ risk preferences. Instead, assuming all else being equal, beneficiary preferences and plan features were held constant, and that the OOP caps affected demand only through changing Medigap premiums. As a result, we were unable to assess certain outcomes (like beneficiaries choosing to drop Medigap coverage altogether if an OOP were implemented) and policy choices (eg, banning Medigap after implementing an OOP cap). However, this modeling limitation attenuates the costs of OOP caps to Medicare, as decreasing Medigap enrollment would increase cost sharing and decrease use. As a result, our modeling approach may overstate the costs of OOP caps to Medicare. Third, our analysis relied on several assumptions about beneficiary behavior, Medigap premiums, and the relative expenses of TM and MA. While some elasticity estimates were quite consistent in the literature (eg, own price elasticity for Medigap and medical care) other estimates were less certain (eg, cross price elasticity between Medigap premiums and MA). Our sensitivity analysis suggested that projected CMS expenditures were most sensitive to assumptions about the elasticity of demand for medical care, followed by assumptions about MA benchmark pass-through and other MA behavioral responses, and least sensitive to assumptions about the own-price elasticity of Medigap demand. In addition, baseline projections of Medicare enrollment and spending were derived from the Medicare Trustees Report. Deviations from these projections could affect estimated model impacts. We also did not consider the role of age and experience rating in Medigap, and how this may affect beneficiary choice and switching. While a more comprehensive analysis would account for state variations in Medigap regulations, sensitivity analysis found that our results were not overly sensitive to assumptions about beneficiary switching.

Fourth, our analysis did not consider heterogeneity across individuals and insurance markets. For instance, the effects of OOP caps are likely to vary across beneficiary income and health status and across different state regulatory regimes with respect to Medigap. Lower-income individuals and those with greater health care needs may benefit disproportionately from OOP caps, although this was not evaluated in our study. Relatedly, beneficiaries who switch supplemental insurance regimes likely differ in unobservable ways from those who do not switch,32 which we did not incorporate into our analysis. We also did not consider the potential dynamic response from MA and Medigap plans to attract beneficiaries in light of OOP caps in TM. Fifth, we did not model the impacts of uncollected liability, instead assuming that beneficiaries would be responsible for all OOP costs. In reality, beneficiaries have the ability to negotiate for lower bills or declare bankruptcy rather than paying large OOP bills. Finally, we did not consider the role of stand-alone Part D plans or the potential dropping of supplemental coverage altogether to limit the complexity of our model.

## Conclusions

Results of this study suggest that introducing an OOP cap in traditional Medicare could substantially reduce beneficiary financial burden but would increase federal Medicare spending. These findings highlight the trade-off between improving financial protection for beneficiaries and the substantial federal costs of extending an OOP limit to traditional Medicare.

# Medicaid Lesser-of Rules and Disparities in Skilled Nursing Facility Quality

**Authors:** Kalli G. Koukounas; Fangli Geng; David C. Grabowksi; Kali S. Thomas; Vince Mor; Momotazur Rahman; Cyrus M. Kosar

**Affiliations:** 1Center for Advancing Health Care Policy Through Research, Brown University School of Public Health, Providence, Rhode Island | 2Center for Gerontology and Health Care Research, Brown University School of Public Health, Providence, Rhode Island | 3Department of Health Care Policy, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 4Center for Equity in Aging, John Hopkins University School of Nursing, Baltimore, Maryland

## Abstract

This cross-sectional study examines admissions of dually eligible Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries to high-quality skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) in states that do and do not fully reimburse Medicare SNF coinsurance.

## Abstract

Are Medicaid lesser-of rules, which allow lower Medicare cost-sharing reimbursements to health care organizations serving dually eligible beneficiaries, associated with reduced access to high-quality skilled nursing facilities (SNFs)?

In this cross-sectional study of 5.1 million discharges from SNFs financed by traditional Medicare, differences in facility resource levels and admission rates to high-rated SNFs were 43% and 54% larger, respectively, in states with lesser-of rules compared with states that fully reimburse Medicare SNF coinsurance.

The findings support addressing state Medicare spending burden without shifting costs to health care organizations who care for dually eligible individuals to enhance access to care for this population.

## Abstract

Individuals dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid have historically faced barriers to accessing high-quality skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) for postacute care. One factor potentially contributing to this disparity is that dually eligible individuals yield lower margins than Medicare-only beneficiaries due to the widespread adoption of lesser-of rules by state Medicaid programs; these rules allow states to provide little to no reimbursement for Medicare coinsurance among these patients.

To examine the association of lesser-of rules with disparities in access to high-quality SNFs between dually eligible and Medicare-only beneficiaries.

This cross-sectional study included discharges from a hospital to an SNF financed by traditional Medicare in the US from January 1, 2018, to December 31, 2022. Discharges of individuals already residing in an SNF before hospitalization were excluded. Data were analyzed between July 1 and December 22, 2025.

States’ lesser-of vs full coinsurance payment policy for dually eligible individuals.

Primary outcomes were admitting SNF dependence level on Medicaid long-term care reimbursement, a proxy for facility resources, and admitting SNF 5-star rating. Adjusted mean differences between dually eligible and non–dually eligible patients were calculated and compared across lesser-of and full-payment states via regressions of each outcome on the interaction between patient dual eligibility and state lesser-of status.

The sample included 5 126 814 SNF discharges (mean [SD] patient age, 79.7 [10.6] years; 60% female). In lesser-of states, SNFs that admitted dually eligible individuals demonstrated higher Medicaid dependence compared with facilities admitting Medicare-only beneficiaries (β [SE], 8.51 [0.03] percentage points [pp]; P < .001), a metric that was 43% smaller in full-payment states (β [SE], −3.63 [0.07] pp; P < .001). For dually eligible individuals in lesser-of states, admittance to high-quality SNFs was lower compared with Medicare-only beneficiaries (β [SE], 9.42 [0.07] pp; P < .001), a metric lower by 54% in full-payment states (β [SE], −5.04 [0.16] pp; P < .001).

This cross-sectional study found that disparities in access to higher-quality SNFs between dually eligible and Medicare-only beneficiaries were larger when states used lesser-of rules for determining Medicare coinsurance reimbursements. Our findings underscore the need for policies that address states’ Medicare spending without shifting costs to health care organizations serving the vulnerable dually eligible population.

## Introduction

Individuals who are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid are a high-risk population characterized by high rates of chronic disease, physical and cognitive impairments, and social stressors.1,2,3 Despite their complex care needs, dually eligible individuals have historically faced barriers to accessing high-quality health care. This issue has been well documented in the skilled nursing facility (SNF) setting; dually eligible individuals are more likely to receive care from SNFs with lower staffing levels, more frequent health violations, and an elevated risk for termination from the Medicare and Medicaid programs.4 Although the payer-based disparity in SNF quality is associated with the large differential in Medicaid and private payment rates for long-term care,5 dually eligible individuals are also less frequently admitted to high-quality SNFs for Medicare-financed postacute care.6,7,8,9

Postacute care in SNFs is a high-risk setting where the stakes for delivering quality care are especially raised for clinically complex populations such as dually eligible individuals.10,11 However, scholars have theorized that high-quality, high-demand SNFs may avoid admitting dually eligible beneficiaries because these patients yield lower Medicare margins than their non–dually eligible counterparts.7 A major driver of this cost disparity is Medicaid lesser-of rules, which allow many states to reduce or eliminate Medicare cost-sharing payments for dually eligible individuals despite their nominal responsibility for these charges.

Cost-sharing accounts for a nontrivial share of Medicare SNF revenues. Beginning on the 21st day of an SNF benefit period, traditional Medicare beneficiaries are responsible for a daily coinsurance of $217 (as of 2026; the coinsurance increased from $168 in 2018 to $195 in 2022).12,13 For dually eligible individuals in states with lesser-of rules, however, Medicaid reimburses SNFs for the lesser value of either (1) the $217 daily coinsurance or (2) the Medicaid reimbursement rate for the service minus the amount Medicare has already paid. For example, if the Medicaid per-diem rate for SNF care on day 21 is $320 and Medicare reimburses $300 before beneficiary cost-sharing, the SNF would receive only a $20 coinsurance from Medicaid rather than the full $217 owed by a non–dually eligible traditional Medicare beneficiary. Because Medicaid payment rates are generally low and frequently fall below Medicare rates even without coinsurance, SNFs across 40 states with lesser-of rules incur consistent bad debt from uncollected coinsurance when providing postacute care to dually eligible individuals.4,14,15,16,17,18 Although bad debts are partially recoverable from Medicare, due to several limitations, the reimbursement mechanism is unlikely to offset the financial burden on SNFs.

In this study, we examined the association of lesser-of rules with payer-based disparities in SNF quality. The federal government originally authorized the use of lesser-of rules to help states balance their Medicaid budgets.19 However, we hypothesized that, by paying SNFs less to care for the clinically complex dual-eligible population, these policies may impede access to high-quality care and exacerbate payer-based disparities in states with lesser-of rules compared with states that fully reimburse SNF coinsurances (ie, full-payment states).

## Methods

This cross-sectional study was approved by the institutional review board of Brown University, which waived informed consent due to the use of deidentified administrative data. This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline.

### Data Sources

We combined several sources of administrative data on Medicare beneficiaries and SNFs. Individual- and encounter-level data included the Medicare Beneficiary Summary File, Medicare Standard Analytic Files, Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, and Minimum Data Set. We supplemented these data with SNF characteristics and quality measures from the Certification and Survey Provider Enhanced Reports (CASPER) database, LTCfocus.org, annual SNF cost reports, and Medicare’s Care Compare website. We used the American Community Survey to obtain zip code tabulation area (ZCTA)–level poverty rates.

### Study Population

We identified all hospitalized traditional Medicare beneficiaries directly discharged to an SNF from January 1, 2018, to December 31, 2022. To focus our analyses on postacute care and the start of a new SNF benefit period, we excluded admissions for individuals who were already residing in an SNF during the 60-day period preceding the claim admission date using the residential history file method.20 We also excluded individuals enrolled in Medicare Advantage (MA) due to the lack of complete MA SNF claims data as well as potential differences in SNF benefit structures and the application of lesser-of rules to the MA population. Race and ethnicity were ascertained from the Research Triangle Institute race and ethnicity variable in the Medicare Master Beneficiary Summary File, and were included to characterize the demographic composition of SNFs across the study cohorts. Categories included American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Hispanic, White, and other (individuals not represented by the other 5 racial and ethnic cohorts [eg, multiracial individuals]) or unknown. We excluded residents of US territories.

### Outcomes

Our primary outcomes were designed to estimate the rate at which dually eligible individuals had access to high-quality, high-resource SNFs. First, the Care Compare overall 5-star rating is a composite measure of SNF staffing levels, inspection results, and performance with respect to multiple patient-level outcomes. Quasi-experimental evidence suggests that admission to facilities with higher star ratings is associated with reduced risk of adverse outcomes.11,21 To enhance the interpretability of our analyses, we created a binary indicator for admission to a 4- or 5-star facility to represent high SNF quality. Second, we used the admitting facility proportion of residents financed by Medicaid recorded in annual CASPER surveys. This measure reflects a facility’s level of dependence on Medicaid long-term care reimbursement and is an established proxy for facility resources.4 As the COVID-19 pandemic prevented consistent CASPER survey collection from 2020 onward, we utilized the Medicaid dependence level recorded in the nearest completed CASPER survey for 2021 and 2022 discharges.

In secondary analyses, we investigated care patterns that may be associated with the reduction in reimbursement generated by lesser-of rules, including rates of within 20-day SNF discharge and 30-day hospital readmission. SNFs in lesser-of states are financially incentivized to discharge dually eligible individuals before cost-sharing begins on the 21st day of care, either to community settings or other facilities such as hospitals.

### Main Explanatory Variables

The main explanatory variables were dual eligibility status and residence in a state with a full-payment or lesser-of rule. We assigned dual eligibility based on individuals’ Medicaid eligibility status in the calendar month preceding SNF admission. Because exact eligibility dates are unknown, lagging by 1 month more accurately assesses an individual’s dual eligibility prior to SNF admission. For our primary analyses, we classified individuals as dually eligible regardless of Medicaid benefit levels (ie, whether they had full benefits with comprehensive Medicaid coverage or partial benefits with Medicaid assistance limited to Medicare premiums or cost-sharing). We addressed Medicaid benefit levels in our sensitivity analyses.

Lesser-of status was derived from reports published by the Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program Payment and Access Commission in 2018 and 2025.22 During our study period, 9 states (Alabama, Arkansas, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, New York, South Dakota, Vermont, and Wisconsin) and the District of Columbia had full-payment policies. All other states were considered to have lesser-of status. Over the course of the study, lesser-of status was consistent for all states with the exception of the District of Columbia, which adopted a full-payment policy in 2019 and, accordingly, was classified as having lesser-of status in 2018 only.

### Control Variables

Demographic controls were derived from the Medicare Beneficiary Summary File and included age, age squared, sex, race and ethnicity, and current Medicare entitlement reason. To capture differences in case mix, we controlled for index hospital length of stay, intensive care unit stay, dementia diagnosis,23 and diagnosis-related group (DRG) fixed effects, all obtained from the Medicare Provider Analysis and Review file. DRGs are a classification scheme for inpatient stays based on principal diagnosis and are severity weighted according to secondary diagnoses. For certain descriptive purposes, we reported the prevalence of DRGs that commonly precipitate after acute care.

### Statistical Analysis

Data were analyzed between July 1 and December 22, 2025. We began our admission-level analyses by graphically presenting crude means of primary outcomes for dually eligible and Medicare-only beneficiaries across neighborhoods, approximated by ZCTAs, in lesser-of and full-payment states. We then estimated adjusted differences in primary and secondary outcomes observed between dually eligible and Medicare-only beneficiaries associated with lesser-of payment policies via ordinary least-squares. Specifically, we regressed each outcome on dual eligibility status, residence in a lesser-of state (reference group) vs a full-payment state, and the interaction between these 2 terms, controlling for the aforementioned covariates and year and state fixed effects. Although state fixed effects were almost perfectly correlated with lesser-of status, our focus was not on the binary lesser-of status coefficient. Instead, our parameters of interest were the coefficients on dual eligibility and the interaction term. Specifically, the dual-eligibility coefficient represents the mean difference in outcomes between dually eligible and Medicare-only SNF residents in lesser-of states, while the interaction term coefficient indicates how payer-based disparities in outcomes differ in full-payment states (ie, a difference in disparities estimate).

We conducted multiple sensitivity analyses. First, we provided estimates excluding state fixed effects. Second, we supplanted state fixed effects with ZCTA fixed effects to specifically assess within-neighborhood payer-based disparities across state types. Third, we limited dually eligible beneficiaries to those in the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary Program, the group consistently covered by full-payment rules. Fourth, we excluded lesser-of states that did not border a full-payment state to enhance comparability. Fifth, we excluded admissions that occurred in 2020 because SNFs were especially affected by the COVID-19 pandemic that year. All analyses were conducted using Stata, version 18.0 (Stata Corp LLC). Null hypotheses were tested assuming a 2-tailed α of .05.

A consequence of lesser-of rules is the generation of bad, or unrecoverable, debt for SNFs providing postacute care to dually eligible individuals. We calculated bad debt burden for all SNFs located in lesser-of states in 2022, defined as total bad debts attributable to dually eligible individuals (specifically itemized in the cost reports) divided by facility bed size from CASPER. We then characterized SNFs according to quartile of bad debt burden, with the highest quartile indicating the greatest bad debt burden.

## Discussion

In this study, we found that disparities in access to high-quality SNFs between dually eligible and non–dually eligible Medicare beneficiaries were greater when states used lesser-of rules for determining cost-sharing reimbursements. In states that fully reimbursed SNF coinsurance amounts, payer-based differences in admissions to highly rated facilities were 54% lower and the disparity in admitting facility Medicaid dependence level was 43% lower. These results suggest that SNFs in full-payment states are less segregated by payer mix than those in lesser-of states; this may result in more resources being available to improve care quality and outcomes.

In our analysis of secondary outcomes, we found that dually eligible individuals, who have more complex care needs, were less likely to be discharged within 20 days compared with Medicare-only beneficiaries in all states. However, the size of this disparity was reduced by 36% in lesser-of states compared with full-payment states, suggesting that loss of point-of-service payments for dually eligible individuals on the 21st day of SNF care may result in higher rates of early discharge than may be appropriate in this population. This finding is consistent with past work documenting high rates of discharge before 21 days among vulnerable patient populations.24 Higher disparities in 30-day readmission rates in lesser-of states may also reflect increased incentives to discharge dually eligible individuals earlier.

The federal government officially authorized lesser-of rules in 1997 to assist states with balancing their budgets.19 The results of this study suggest that this practice may negatively impact dually eligible individuals’ access to high-quality care, which can lead to further costs downstream. For SNFs, a direct consequence of lesser-of rules is the accumulation of bad debt from unpaid or underpaid coinsurances. Although bad debts are recoverable through a Medicare reimbursement mechanism, this is unlikely to offset the consequences of lesser-of policies for at least 3 reasons. First, Medicare reimburses only 65% of bad debts, and several proposals have aimed to further reduce or even eliminate bad debt reimbursement entirely.25 Second, because bad debts are reimbursed after the fiscal year ends, SNFs lose revenue at the point of service, constraining their operational capacity. Third, there are administrative costs to seeking bad debt reimbursement from Medicare. Notably, in our study, SNFs most burdened by bad debt had exceedingly low quality ratings, high numbers of deficiency citations, and disproportionately served racial and ethnic minority groups.

Although lesser-of rules have been widely used across states for many years, their role in health care access and delivery has been underresearched, especially outside primary care settings.16,26,27 To our knowledge, this study is the first to focus on lesser-of rules in the SNF setting and extends the literature on payer-based disparities in SNF quality. In past research, low Medicaid long-term care reimbursement rates have been consistently associated with lower SNF quality for dually eligible individuals.4,28,29 Regarding postacute care, scholars have theorized that SNFs potentially avoid admitting dually eligible individuals due to the risk of them becoming long-stay residents, which causes a sharp drop in revenues as the payer switches from Medicare to Medicaid.7,9,30 Our results are consistent with this theory, as dually eligible individuals were admitted to lower-quality SNFs in both lesser-of and full-payment states. However, our analysis identified lesser-of rules as an additional contributor because payer-based disparities were magnified in states with these policies.

Improving health care delivery to dually eligible individuals has been an ongoing policy priority. Contemporary reforms have largely focused on the coordination of Medicaid and Medicare benefits, especially through the MA program. Proposals related to shifting dually eligible individuals’ cost-sharing burden from Medicaid to Medicare, which could address the burden of lesser-of rules, have not yet gained traction.31 Our results underscore the importance of these proposals, particularly because states are unlikely to adopt full-payment policies in the current fiscally austere environment for Medicaid.

### Limitations

This study has limitations. First, our results cannot be generalized to the MA program. Although lesser-of rules may impact SNF care for MA enrollees, the mechanisms are less clear due to potential differences in SNF benefit structures and bad debt reimbursement processes across MA plans. Second, the use of lesser-of or full-payment rules may be correlated with other Medicaid policies that are more or less favorable to dually eligible individuals in the SNF setting. Although we cannot rule out this possibility, it is worth noting the geographic diversity of Medicaid programs with full-payment policies. Third, although we used a carefully constructed postacute cohort with controls with strong health status, there may have been unobserved payer-based differences in health status across lesser-of and full-payment states that confounded our cross-sectional estimates.

## Conclusions

In this cross-sectional study of 5.1 million discharges to SNFs, compared with Medicare-only beneficiaries, dually eligible individuals in lesser-of states experienced higher rates of admission to lower-quality facilities with fewer resources as well as earlier discharge and modestly increased readmission rates. While lesser-of rules are intended to lower state Medicaid expenditures, this policy may have unintended consequences for dually eligible individuals and ultimately lead to additional costs downstream. These findings underscore the need for policies that address state Medicare spending without shifting costs to the health care organizations serving the vulnerable dually eligible population.

# Trends in hospital discharge outcomes among high-risk Medicare beneficiaries before and during the COVID-19 pandemic

**Authors:** Anthony I Roberts; Christopher M Santostefano; Zihan Chen; Brian E McGarry; Elizabeth M White; Linda J Resnik; Fangli Geng; David C Grabowski; Momotazur Rahman

**Affiliations:** Department of Health Services, Policy, and Practice, Brown University School of Public Health, Providence, RI 02903, United States | Division of Geriatrics and Aging, Department of Medicine, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY 14642, United States | Department of Health Care Policy, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, United States

## Abstract

Medicare beneficiaries face significant health risks and care disruptions during public health emergencies, but little is known about how care patterns evolved throughout the COVID-19 pandemic or differed between traditional Medicare (TM) and Medicare Advantage (MA).

Using Medicare claims data for over 20 million hospital discharges during 2018-2022, we examined trends in hospital length of stay, discharge disposition, and mortality among beneficiaries with 5 major comorbidities (dementia, diabetes, congestive heart failure, hip fracture, and stroke), stratified by COVID status and payer type.

We found that COVID patients initially experienced substantially longer hospital stays (8.3 vs 4.6 days) and higher 30-day mortality (34% vs 5%) compared to patients without COVID. MA beneficiaries showed consistently higher home health utilization but similar mortality patterns to TM enrollees. By mid-2022, most outcome differences had converged between COVID and non-COVID patients, suggesting health system adaptation to the pandemic.

Our findings highlight how the pandemic was associated with shifts toward home-based post-acute care, emphasizing the need for policies supporting home-based care infrastructure and flexible care delivery models that could help health systems better adapt during future public health emergencies.

## Introduction

The COVID-19 pandemic significantly disrupted healthcare delivery and outcomes for older adults, one of the most vulnerable populations to the virus.1,2 Prior studies have highlighted the pandemic's impact on hospital-based care,3-5 documenting increased mortality rates,6,7 and notable changes in discharge disposition patterns among the Medicare population.4,8,9 However, several important knowledge gaps remain in our understanding of how hospital care delivery and post-acute care transitions evolved from the height of the pandemic and as the pandemic waned.

Medicare beneficiaries, who account for approximately 19% of the U.S. population but represented nearly 80% of COVID-19 deaths during the initial waves of the pandemic, faced unique challenges during the pandemic.10,11 Early reports documented substantial disruptions in care access, with hospital admission volumes dropping by 32%-43% during March-April 2020 compared to pre-pandemic levels.3,12 These disruptions particularly affected older adults with chronic conditions requiring ongoing medical management, heightening concerns about care quality and continuity for this population.13,14

Post-acute care utilization patterns also shifted dramatically during the pandemic.8 A notable change was a shift away from post-acute care provided in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs), toward home-based care. Early in the pandemic, discharges to SNFs decreased (from roughly 19% of Medicare hospital discharges in 2019 to about 14% in late 2020), while discharges home with home health care rose, making home health the dominant post-acute care setting by mid-2020.8,15 These shifts were influenced by multiple factors, including infection concerns in congregate settings, workforce shortages, and changing patient and provider preferences. Although some rebound in SNF admissions for post-acute care has occurred, evidence suggests the pandemic accelerated a preexisting trend toward utilization of home-based care.8 Importantly, while discharge dispositions to SNFs began to rebound by 2022, it remains unclear whether this recovery was uniform across all patient populations and payer types, particularly for high-risk individuals with complex chronic conditions who often require more intensive post-acute care services.15

Even before the pandemic, Medicare post-acute care utilization was undergoing significant transformation due to payment policy changes. In October 2019, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) implemented the Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) for SNFs, which shifted from therapy volume-based payments to a case-mix classification system based on patient characteristics.16 Similarly, in January 2020, CMS introduced the Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) for home health, replacing the previous episode-based payment approach with a patient needs-based system.17 These reforms created financial incentives that likely influenced discharge patterns. For instance, PDPM encouraged SNFs to admit more medically complex patients while shortening lengths of stay, while PDGM restructured home health payments based on patient characteristics rather than service volume.18 The timing of these payment reforms, implemented just before or during the early stages of the pandemic, creates an important backdrop for understanding the evolution of discharge disposition patterns during this period.

While prior research has explored overall COVID-19 effects on healthcare utilization and outcomes, less is known about how these trends differed between patients hospitalized with and without COVID or between traditional Medicare (TM) beneficiaries and Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollees. With over half of all Medicare beneficiaries being enrolled in MA,19 understanding differences in care patterns and outcomes between these payer types is increasingly important for Medicare policy development. Historical evidence indicates that MA enrollees typically receive less post-acute care overall, including fewer days in SNFs, lower use of inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and reduced home health care utilization, compared to TM beneficiaries, yet experience lower hospital readmission rates and higher rates of successful discharge to the community.20,21 Given these historical differences, MA plans, with their capitated payment structure, flexible benefit design and incentives to manage utilization, may have been able to respond differently than TM to pandemic-related challenges.22

Additionally, most existing studies have focused on the acute phase of the pandemic (2020-2021), with limited investigation into how trends evolved as healthcare systems adapted and the pandemic waned.8 Understanding these longer-term patterns is crucial for informing health system resilience and preparedness for future public health emergencies.

This study aims to address these knowledge gaps by examining trends in hospital length of stay, discharge disposition patterns, and mortality outcomes among Medicare beneficiaries with 5 common and high-risk conditions: dementia, diabetes, congestive heart failure (CHF), hip fracture, and stroke. Using Medicare claims data from 2018 to 2022, we examined how these outcomes differed by COVID-19 status and Medicare payer type, and how these patterns evolved throughout the pandemic period.

## Methods

### Study population and data

We analyzed unique hospital discharges identified using the Medicare Provider Analysis and Review (MedPAR) file, between January 2018 and December 2022. MedPAR aggregates inpatient claims to the stay-level for 100% of Medicare beneficiaries who had an inpatient admission to an acute care, rehabilitation, or psychiatric hospital. Claims were linked to the Master Beneficiary Summary File (MBSF) using unique patient identifiers to obtain demographics, MA enrollment in a given month, Medicaid eligibility, and the date of death. We classified beneficiaries as MA enrollees if they were enrolled in an MA plan during the month of their hospital discharge. The study included beneficiaries Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 and older who were discharged with at least one of the following diagnoses documented during their hospitalization: Alzheimer's disease or related dementias, diabetes, CHF, hip fracture, or stroke. Diagnoses were identified from all 25 diagnosis fields in the MedPAR record of the index hospitalization using the enhanced Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) code algorithms published in 2020.23 While all beneficiaries in the sample qualified for Medicare based on age, a small proportion (<2%) also qualified through end-stage renal disease entitlement. We excluded beneficiaries who had used inpatient services in the previous 6 months to focus on incident hospitalizations. COVID-19 status was determined using ICD-10 diagnosis codes documented in any of the 25 diagnosis fields in MedPAR during the index hospitalization. Following the approach used by CMS, we used codes U07.1 and B97.29 prior to the introduction of code U07.1 in April 2020, and U07.1 only from April 2020 onward.24 We defined the pandemic period as beginning in March 2020 during the first U.S. wave.

### Key measures

Our outcomes include hospital length of stay (days between the date of admission and discharge), discharge destination identified on the inpatient claim (home/self-care, skilled nursing facility, home health services, or inpatient rehabilitation facility), and 30-day all-cause mortality (assessed using MBSF death dates).

### Analytic approach

We estimated trends in monthly discharge dispositions using regression models to generate risk-adjusted probabilities of an outcome in each month, controlling for age, sex, race, dual eligibility status, Charlson Comorbidity Index computed from hospital diagnoses, the aforementioned comorbidity diagnoses, and hospital fixed effects. The models included interaction terms between month-year and payer type, and between month-year and COVID-19 status, allowing us to estimate differential trends by payer type and COVID-19 diagnosis. We used linear regression for hospital length of stay and logit models for binary outcomes.

### Limitations

Our results should be interpreted within the context of certain limitations. First, while we controlled for observable patient characteristics and hospital fixed effects, unobserved differences between MA and TM beneficiaries may influence our findings. Second, our analysis focused on beneficiaries with specific comorbidities, and results may not generalize to the broader Medicare population. Third, because our identification of comorbidities relies on Medicare claims data, it may be subject to coding differences between TM and MA. Given that MA plans have been shown to exhibit higher coding intensity, it is possible that some observed differences in comorbidity burden reflect differential coding rather than true clinical differences.25,26 Fourth, our study relies on MedPAR data, which likely undercounts MA beneficiary hospitalizations because hospitals don't directly bill CMS for these stays. While we used MBSF enrollment data to classify MA status, the underlying sample may not fully represent all MA hospitalizations. This reporting bias varies by hospital characteristics and service types, and the extent of underreporting remains uncertain, as noted in MedPAC analyses.27 Finally, our data cannot fully capture the impact of important factors like vaccination status or specific therapeutic interventions that emerged during the pandemic.

## Results

From January 2018 to December 2022, we observed 20 991 657 hospital discharges of Medicare beneficiaries with dementia, diabetes, CHF, hip fracture, or stroke, including 1 123 615 discharges for patients with COVID (Table 1). Patient characteristics and outcomes differed between the pre-pandemic and pandemic periods. Compared to all pre-pandemic patients, COVID patients were more likely to be dual-eligible (30% vs 23%) and have diabetes (64% vs 57%); and were less likely to have a stroke (4.6% vs 9.5%) or hip fracture (2.1% vs 6.4%), or be discharged home with self-care (34% vs 43%). COVID patients experienced longer hospital stays (mean, 8.7 vs 5.1 days), were more likely to require intensive care unit admission (40% vs 33%), and had nearly triple the 30-day mortality rate (27% vs 9.7%) than pre-pandemic patients. (Table 1). Total discharge volume dropped during the initial wave of the pandemic, reaching a low of 238 000 discharges in April 2020 compared to typical monthly discharges of 340 000-370 000 pre-pandemic (Figure S1). The share of discharged patients with the 5 diagnoses remained relatively stable from the pre-pandemic to pandemic periods, with diabetes being the most common diagnosis (56%-58%) (Figure S2).

However, MA enrollees exhibited similar trends to TM enrollees throughout the study period.

## Discussion

Our analysis of over 20 million hospital discharges highlights key differences in discharge dispositions and outcomes between hospitalized Medicare beneficiaries with and without COVID-19 before and during the pandemic. During the pandemic, COVID patients experienced longer hospital stays, lower likelihood of discharge to home with self-care, and higher mortality rates compared to patients without COVID. However, these patterns for the 2 groups generally converged by the second quarter of 2022. Additionally, we observed significant shifts in post-acute care utilization patterns, with a notable transition toward home health care that began to converge between COVID and non-COVID patients by early 2021, coinciding with the widespread availability of COVID-19 vaccines.

A key contribution of this study is the observation of differences in outcomes for MA enrollees and TM beneficiaries. While both MA and TM beneficiaries showed similar overall trends, MA enrollees, both those with and without COVID, on average experienced modestly longer hospital stays. Additionally, MA beneficiaries demonstrated higher utilization of home health services compared to TM beneficiaries, whereas TM enrollees had greater use of inpatient rehabilitation facilities. Interestingly, this finding contrasts with earlier studies that have found MA enrollees to have lower rates of home health care, attributed to more restrictive prior authorization processes and frequent recertification requirements for home health services.29-32 This contrast could be driven by our focus on hospitalizations with 5 selected comorbidities. The differences in discharge disposition patterns between MA and TM beneficiaries, even during a public health crisis, suggest that program-level incentives and care management approaches may influence service use.

Mortality rates among hospitalized COVID patients fluctuated over time, declining significantly after the first wave of the pandemic as knowledge and therapeutics for inpatient management of COVID-19 improved, and then again with the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines in December 2020.33 Mortality increased again during the Delta variant surge in the summer of 2021,34 and then declined again in late 2021 and early 2022 with the emergence of the Omicron variants which were more contagious but less lethal than prior strains.35 Other factors, including broader population immunity due both to vaccination and natural infection and improved clinical management of COVID-19, including the emergence of antivirals and monoclonal antibodies, contributed to this transition to the “new normal.”36-39 Importantly, the similar mortality patterns observed among MA and TM beneficiaries, despite some differences in post-acute care use, suggest that insurance type had little influence on mortality, underscoring the dominant clinical impact of COVID-19 on high-risk populations regardless of payer type.

Our study also identified a significant shift in post-acute care patterns. Comparing before and after the pandemic, we observed a decline in discharges to SNF, decreasing from 11.9% to 9.6% among non-COVID patients. Concurrently, the proportion of patients discharged to home—both with and without home health care—increased. These findings point to a broader trend away from SNFs during the pandemic, likely driven by concerns about infection risk and evolving care preferences.9

These trends in discharge patterns have several policy implications for Medicare. First, the shift toward home-based post-acute care highlights the need for appropriate infrastructure and reimbursement to support post-acute care in the home setting.40,41 The recent change in Medicare's home health payment model to the PDGM, which shifted reimbursement to be based on patient clinical characteristics rather than service volume, needs ongoing evaluation to ensure it incentivizes appropriate home-based care for high-risk patients.42 Second, access to telehealth and remote monitoring services could potentially help support safe transitions to home for certain patients with chronic illness. During the pandemic, CMS temporarily expanded telehealth coverage, allowing providers to virtually engage patients at home when in-person visits posed risks​.43 Making some of these telehealth flexibilities permanent, with appropriate safeguards and ongoing evaluation of their effectiveness, may help improve continuity of care for recently discharged patients by enabling timely virtual check-ins, monitoring of symptoms, and follow-up consultations​. Third, investment in the home-based care workforce is critical. The pandemic exacerbated nationwide shortages of nurses, therapists, home health aides, and other direct care workers, straining the capacity of home health providers.44 Policymakers may need to bolster workforce development programs and incentives to attract and retain qualified home health professionals. For example, several states have used American Rescue Plan Act funds and Medicaid waivers to strengthen their direct care workforce, and similar investment strategies could be considered within Medicare (or through cross-payer initiatives) to ensure an adequate supply of home-based care services for Medicare beneficiaries.45

Our findings also highlight the importance of having comprehensive discharge and transitional care plans in place for both TM and MA populations, particularly those with chronic illness after hospitalization for COVID-19. Value-based care initiatives like the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program incentivize improved discharge planning and care coordination for conditions common in our study cohort.46 Policy efforts could focus on strengthening evidence-based discharge planning and post-discharge follow-up across both payment models, perhaps by enhancing reimbursement for transitional care management services. Ultimately, our findings suggest that quality of care transitions, rather than payer type, are associated with outcomes for vulnerable patient populations during public health emergencies.

In conclusion, our analysis highlights the evolving impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on hospital discharge dispositions and post-acute care patterns among Medicare beneficiaries. While differences between COVID and non-COVID patients attenuated over time, the pandemic accelerated a shift away from post-acute care provided in SNFs toward home-based care. These findings underscore the need for continued monitoring and adaptive health policies to support vulnerable populations in the face of future public health challenges.
